'''Lucien Hardy''' (born 1966) is a British-Canadian [[theoretical physics|theoretical]] [[physicist]] currently based at the [[Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics]] in [[Waterloo, Ontario|Waterloo, Canada]]. 

Hardy is best known for his work on the [[Quantum foundations|foundation]] of [[quantum physics]], including the [[Hardy's paradox]] thought experiment, and his influential work in [[quantum field theory]], which seeks to reconcile [[quantum mechanics]] to [[general relativity]].<ref name="ludmer">{{cite web |last1=Clark |first1=Joanne |title=Lucien Hardy: Thought, Matter, and Quantum Theory |url=http://ludmercentre.ca/lucien-hardy-thought-matter-and-quantum-theory/ |website=The Ludmer Centre |access-date=6 May 2023 |language=en-CA |date=25 March 2019}}</ref><ref name=quanta />

==Education==
Hardy studied for his doctorate at [[Durham University]] (1989–1992) under the supervision of Euan J. Squires.<ref name="mathgene">{{MathGenealogy|id=204149}}</ref>

==Work==
In 1992, he became lecturer in [[mathematical physics]] at [[Maynooth College]], part of The [[National University of Ireland]]. He was subsequently a Royal Society postdoctoral fellow at the [[University of Innsbruck]] (1993–1994), then returned to Durham as Lecturer (1994–1996), and was a postdoctoral fellow at [[La Sapienza University]] (1996–1997).<ref name="perimeterprofile">{{cite web |title=Lucien Hardy |url=https://perimeterinstitute.ca/people/lucien-hardy |website=Perimeter Institute |access-date=6 May 2023 |language=en}}</ref>

Starting in 1997, he was a Royal Society University Research Fellow at the [[University of Oxford]] until 2002.<ref name=perimeterprofile />

Hardy is now affiliated with the [[University of Waterloo]] and is among the faculty of the [[Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics]].<ref name=perimeterprofile />

===Hardy's paradox===
In 1992, Hardy published a [[thought experiment]] that "makes nonsense of the famous interaction between [[matter]] and [[antimatter]]" — that when a [[particle]] meets its [[antiparticle]], the pair "always annihilate one another" in a burst of energy.<ref name="economist">{{cite news |title=I'm not looking, honest! |url=https://www.economist.com/science-and-technology/2009/03/05/im-not-looking-honest |newspaper=[[The Economist]] |access-date=6 May 2023 |date=7 March 2009}}</ref> Hardy proposed the possibility that in some cases when said interaction is not observed a particle and an antiparticle could interact with one another and survive. But since the interaction has to remain unseen, no one would notice this happening, which is why the result came to be known as [[Hardy's paradox]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hardy |first=Lucien |title=Quantum mechanics, local realistic theories, and Lorentz-invariant realistic theories |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=68 |issue=20 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.68.2981 |pages=2981–2984 |year=1992 |pmid=10045577 |bibcode=1992PhRvL..68.2981H}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hardy |first=Lucien |title=Nonlocality for two particles without inequalities for almost all entangled states |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=71 |issue=11 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.71.1665 |pages=1665–1668 |year=1993 |pmid=10054467 |bibcode=1993PhRvL..71.1665H}}</ref><ref name=economist />

===''Quantum Theory From Five Reasonable Axioms''===
In 2001, Hardy published ''Quantum Theory From Five Reasonable Axioms'', a paper that offered an axiomatic reconstruction of quantum theory. His proposal represented an "operational" approach made famous by [[Albert Einstein]], but applied to [[quantum mechanics]].<ref name="quanta">{{cite web |last1=Wolchover |first1=Natalie |title=Quantum Mischief Rewrites the Laws of Cause and Effect |url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/quantum-mischief-rewrites-the-laws-of-cause-and-effect-20210311/ |website=Quanta |access-date=6 May 2023 |date=11 March 2021}}</ref> 

In subsequent years, other authors built upon Hardy's work by proposing their own variants.<ref>{{cite arXiv|last=Hardy|first=Lucien|date=2001-01-03|title=Quantum Theory From Five Reasonable Axioms|eprint=quant-ph/0101012 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Darrigol |first1=Olivier |title='Shut up and contemplate!': Lucien Hardy׳s reasonable axioms for quantum theory |journal=Studies in History and Philosophy of Science Part B: Studies in History and Philosophy of Modern Physics |date=November 2015 |volume=52, Part B |pages=328–342 |doi=10.1016/j.shpsb.2015.10.002 |bibcode=2015SHPMP..52..328D }}</ref>
